definition: A finite sequence of well-defined, computer-implementable instructions to solve a specific problem or perform a computation.
technical_context: Fundamental building block of software engineering, analyzed via asymptotic time and space complexity.
example_usage: Dijkstra's algorithm calculates the shortest path in a weighted graph.
linguistic_notes: Candidate sign combines STEP-BY-STEP sequence with LOGIC-PLANNING handshapes; currently under peer review.
handshape: Flat B-Handshape stepping down sequentially
location: Neutral space in front of torso
non_manual_markers: Focused gaze, slight forward head tilt
source_institution: ISLRTC Reference Standard / Academic Syllabus Candidate

definition: An organized, structured collection of digital data stored and accessed electronically from a computer system.
technical_context: Managed by Database Management Systems (DBMS) utilizing SQL for relational ACID-compliant transactions.
example_usage: The PostgreSQL database maintains relational integrity through foreign key constraints.
linguistic_notes: Verified pan-Indian standard sign depicting stacked disk cylinders with horizontal spatial index.
handshape: Bent-C hands shaping cylindrical tiers
movement: Stacking motion from bottom to top tier
orientation: Palms facing inward shaping cylinder boundaries

definition: System software that manages computer hardware, software resources, and provides common services for computer programs.
technical_context: Controls processor scheduling, virtual memory management, file systems, and hardware I/O drivers.
example_usage: The operating system schedules processes using priority-based preemptive algorithms.
linguistic_notes: Compound sign (COMPUTER + SYSTEM-MANAGE); complex kernel mechanics require pedagogical visual diagramming.
handshape: Open-5 hands transitioning to interlocking C-shapes
orientation: Palms facing center with inward rotation

definition: The primary component of a computer that executes instructions comprising a computer program.
technical_context: Fetches, decodes, and executes instructions through an arithmetic logic unit (ALU), control unit (CU), and registers.
example_usage: A multi-core processor executes concurrent threads in parallel.
linguistic_notes: Sign initialized with central chip positioning; clock cycle execution is signed contextually.
handshape: Index and middle fingers extended forming rectangular chip contact
movement: Tapping contact on non-dominant palm followed by outward calculation flutter
orientation: Dominant palm down, non-dominant palm up

definition: Internal storage area in a computer used to store data and instructions that the processor can access directly and quickly.
technical_context: Volatile semiconductor storage organized in addressable bytes directly mapped into processor virtual address spaces.
example_usage: The operating system allocates virtual memory pages to active user processes.
linguistic_notes: Standard ISL sign distinguishing hardware RAM storage from psychological recall by indexing hardware base.
handshape: Modified L-handshape indicating storage grid
orientation: Palms facing down toward horizontal plane

definition: A digital telecommunications network that allows compute nodes to share data and computing resources.
technical_context: Governed by the OSI 7-layer model and TCP/IP stack using packet switching architectures.
example_usage: Routers forward packets across the computer network based on IP routing tables.
linguistic_notes: Interlocking fingertips depicting interconnected distributed nodes in signing space.
handshape: Open-5 hands with fingertips meeting and linking
movement: Oscillating link-and-spread motion across horizontal space
non_manual_markers: Spatial indexing to left and right loci

definition: The process of designing and building an executable computer program to accomplish a specific computing result.
technical_context: Includes syntax analysis, logic structuring, unit testing, and compilation into executable binaries.
example_usage: Object-oriented programming promotes code reusability through inheritance and encapsulation.
linguistic_notes: Standard sign combining typewriter keystroke mimicry with structured vertical line formatting.
handshape: Curved claw hands fluttering fingers
movement: Rapid alternating finger articulation over non-dominant virtual screen

definition: A situation in concurrent computing where two or more competing actions are each waiting for the other to finish, preventing any from proceeding.
technical_context: Requires four Coffman conditions: mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, and circular wait.
example_usage: Deadlock prevention eliminates circular wait conditions using strict resource ordering.
linguistic_notes: Zero-Fabrication Policy: No certified single-sign ISL equivalent exists. Certified educators recommend fingerspelling D-E-A-D-L-O-C-K followed by a circular wait interaction diagram.

definition: A collection of instructions, data, or programs used to operate computers and execute specific tasks.
technical_context: Contrasted with physical hardware; resides in digital storage as bytecode or native machine code.
example_usage: System software abstracts low-level hardware intricacies from user applications.
linguistic_notes: Established ISL sign: dominant 'S' shape gliding across non-dominant palm.
handshape: S-handshape
movement: Smooth horizontal glide across open non-dominant palm
orientation: Dominant palm down, non-dominant palm up

definition: The physical parts or components of a computer, such as the monitor, processor, memory, and motherboard.
technical_context: Includes digital electronic circuitry, silicon microchips, and electromechanical peripherals.
example_usage: Hardware interrupts signal the processor to handle time-critical I/O events.
linguistic_notes: Established ISL sign: dominant fist contacting firm non-dominant forearm to denote physical solidity.
handshape: Closed S-fist contacting open forearm

definition: The process of converting information or data into a code, especially to prevent unauthorized access.
technical_context: Uses mathematical cryptographic algorithms (AES, RSA) and key pairs to transform plaintext into ciphertext.
example_usage: End-to-end encryption ensures that only communicating parties can decrypt messages.
linguistic_notes: Candidate sign: Open text handshape folding into an interlocking key lock.
handshape: Open-C hands closing to interlocked fist

definition: A computer program that translates computer code written in one programming language into another language.
technical_context: Performs lexical analysis, syntax parsing, semantic checking, intermediate code generation, optimization, and code synthesis.
example_usage: The compiler transforms high-level C++ source code into optimized machine binaries.
linguistic_notes: Candidate sign: Text lines entering processing funnel and emerging as structured binary.
handshape: Flat-B transitioning through funnel shape to index point

definition: A specialized format for organizing, processing, retrieving, and storing data efficiently in memory.
technical_context: Includes linear structures (arrays, linked lists, stacks, queues) and non-linear structures (trees, graphs, hash tables).
example_usage: Selecting the optimal data structure reduces algorithm lookup complexity to O(1).
linguistic_notes: Compound sign: DATA (digital pulses) + STRUCTURE (arranged hierarchical blocks).
handshape: Bent-B hands forming rectangular grid cells

definition: On-demand availability of computer system resources, especially data storage and computing power, without direct active management by the user.
technical_context: Includes IaaS, PaaS, SaaS delivery models over public, private, or hybrid virtualized multi-tenant clusters.
example_usage: Cloud computing enables automated elastic autoscaling during web traffic surges.
linguistic_notes: Established sign: CLOUD morphology with dynamic server communication fingers.
handshape: Curved claw hands shaping cloud perimeter
movement: Puffing circular trace outward, then down-pointing wireless rays
location: Above head level down to chest
orientation: Palms facing each other then down

definition: A high-speed data storage layer which stores a subset of data, typically transient, so future requests are served faster.
technical_context: L1, L2, and L3 SRAM caches located on-die with the processor core to minimize memory latency bottlenecks.
example_usage: Cache misses force the processor to access slower DRAM main memory.
linguistic_notes: Candidate sign: Quick-access pocket positioned directly adjacent to central processor locus.
handshape: Flat-C hand grasping rapid sliver
movement: Swift inward snap into pocket space

definition: The smallest sequence of programmed instructions that can be managed independently by a scheduler.
technical_context: Threads within the same process share code, data, and open file descriptors while maintaining separate program counters and stacks.
example_usage: Multithreading enables responsive user interfaces while executing background tasks.
linguistic_notes: Contextual disambiguation: Must not be confused with sewing textile thread. Distinguishes concurrent process line.
handshape: Index fingers extended as thin parallel execution tracks

definition: A programming language object that stores the memory address of another value located in computer memory.
technical_context: Crucial for dynamic memory allocation, array navigation, and passing structures by reference in C/C++.
example_usage: Dereferencing a null pointer results in a segmentation fault.
linguistic_notes: Zero-Fabrication Policy: Requires fingerspelling P-O-I-N-T-E-R and spatial indexing to target address block.

definition: A memory management capability of an operating system that uses hardware and software to allow a computer to compensate for physical memory shortages.
technical_context: Employs hardware Memory Management Units (MMU), page tables, and Translation Lookaside Buffers (TLB) for demand paging.
example_usage: Virtual memory maps isolated linear address spaces to contiguous or fragmented physical frames.
linguistic_notes: Compound sign: VIRTUAL (imagined/abstract) + MEMORY. Requires visual paging explanation.
handshape: Open-5 fingers spreading into abstract space over RAM base

definition: A method of solving a computational problem where the solution depends on solutions to smaller instances of the same problem.
technical_context: Functions that call themselves repeatedly until reaching a designated base case that terminates stack unwinding.
example_usage: Merge sort utilizes recursion to divide arrays into smaller subarrays.
linguistic_notes: Candidate sign: Circular looping motion feeding back into the origin handshape.
handshape: Index finger pointing back toward dominant wrist

definition: An abstract data type that serves as a collection of elements, with two principal operations: push and pop (Last-In, First-Out).
technical_context: Used in runtime memory management to track function activation records, local variables, and return addresses.
example_usage: Exceeding allocated call stack depth produces a stack overflow error.
linguistic_notes: Spatial classifier representing vertical plate stacking (PUSH onto top, POP from top).
handshape: Flat-B hands horizontally oriented
movement: Placing dominant hand atop non-dominant hand repeatedly

definition: The difference in electric potential between two points, representing the work needed per unit of charge to move a test charge between them.
technical_context: Measured in Volts (V); drives electrical current through a closed circuit according to Ohm's Law (V = IR).
example_usage: A voltage drop occurs as current flows across the resistor.
linguistic_notes: Standard ISL sign: 'V' handshape indicating electrical pressure potential across spatial poles.
handshape: V-handshape
movement: Direct pulsed forward thrust between positive and negative spatial loci

definition: The rate of flow of electric charge past a point or region in an electrical circuit.
technical_context: Contextual Disambiguation: Distinguishes electrical charge flow (Amperes) from temporal 'current events' or oceanic current.
example_usage: Alternating current reverses its direction periodically at 50 Hz.
linguistic_notes: Continuous horizontal stream gesture along wire axis depicting electron drift velocity.
handshape: Bent-claw hands oscillating horizontally along directional pathway
movement: Continuous directional flow from right to left locus
orientation: Palms facing downward along circuit track

definition: A measure of the opposition to current flow in an electrical circuit, measured in Ohms.
technical_context: Dissipates electrical energy as heat in accordance with Joule's First Law (P = I^2 * R).
example_usage: High resistance in the conductor causes significant power loss.
linguistic_notes: Established sign: Hand resisting/blocking forward flow of current across wire barrier.
handshape: Dominant flat palm pressing firmly against incoming non-dominant current stream
non_manual_markers: Tense cheek/jaw morpheme indicating resistance force

definition: The ratio of the change in an electric charge in a system to the corresponding change in its electric potential.
technical_context: Measured in Farads (F); stores potential energy in an electrostatic field between conductive plates separated by a dielectric.
example_usage: Capacitors in parallel add their total capacitance values directly.
linguistic_notes: Candidate sign: Parallel plates holding electrostatic charge buffer in between.
handshape: Flat-B hands parallel to each other
movement: Approaching parallel motion without physical contact, pulsing charge

definition: The tendency of an electrical conductor to oppose a change in the electric current flowing through it.
technical_context: Measured in Henries (H); induces electromotive force (EMF) via Faraday's Law of Induction proportional to dI/dt.
example_usage: Inductance in the transmission line causes inductive reactance.
linguistic_notes: Candidate sign: Spiral coiled wire motion surrounding a magnetic core axis.
handshape: Curved index finger tracing coiled spiral

definition: A closed loop that allows electrons or current to travel continuous paths through interconnected components.
technical_context: Analyzed using Kirchhoff's Current Law (KCL) and Kirchhoff's Voltage Law (KVL).
example_usage: A short circuit creates a low-resistance path, drawing excessive current.
linguistic_notes: Looping boundary sign tracing a closed rectangular electrical loop in signing space.
handshape: Index fingers meeting at top and tracing continuous closed perimeter
movement: Perimeter tracing meeting at bottom terminal

definition: A two-terminal electronic component that conducts current primarily in one direction (asymmetric conductance).
technical_context: Features low forward resistance and high reverse resistance across a doped p-n junction.
example_usage: A bridge rectifier uses four diodes to convert AC into DC.
linguistic_notes: Candidate sign: Arrowhead passing forward through vertical barrier plate.
handshape: Dominant V/arrow pointing through non-dominant flat barrier
orientation: Dominant palm forward, non-dominant palm inward

definition: A semiconductor device used to amplify or switch electrical signals and power.
technical_context: Three-terminal device (Base/Gate, Collector/Drain, Emitter/Source); fundamental foundation of modern digital microchips.
example_usage: Billions of MOSFET transistors are integrated onto modern microprocessors.
linguistic_notes: Candidate sign: Three-terminal gate controlling main current throughput.
handshape: Three fingers extended (E-B-C) with gating pulse

definition: An integrated circuit that contains all the functions of a central processing unit of a computer on a single microchip.
technical_context: Includes address, data, and control buses interfacing with external ROM, RAM, and I/O peripherals.
example_usage: The 8086 microprocessor features a 16-bit architecture and a 1 MB addressable memory space.
linguistic_notes: Candidate sign: Pin-grid array chip indexed with fast binary processing streams.
handshape: Fingertips forming small square chip boundary
movement: Placement onto circuit board followed by clock pulse

definition: A function that conveys information about the state or behavior of a physical system, typically represented as time-varying voltage.
technical_context: Analyzed in time and frequency domains using Fourier and Laplace transformations.
example_usage: Fourier transforms decompose a continuous time signal into its constituent frequency spectrum.
linguistic_notes: Sinusoidal wave oscillation moving forward across horizontal transmission axis.
handshape: Index finger or open flat hand tracing sine wave undulating peaks and troughs
movement: Smooth sinusoidal wave motion progressing outward

definition: The number of occurrences of a repeating event per unit of time, measured in Hertz (cycles per second).
technical_context: Inversely proportional to period (f = 1/T); determines spectral band allocations in RF communications.
example_usage: The carrier frequency for FM radio broadcasts ranges from 88 to 108 MHz.
linguistic_notes: Rapid rhythmic periodic oscillation indicating cycle count per second.
handshape: Bent-index finger pulsing cycles

definition: The process of varying one or more properties of a periodic waveform, called the carrier signal, with an information-bearing modulating signal.
technical_context: Includes Amplitude Modulation (AM), Frequency Modulation (FM), and digital schemes like QPSK and QAM.
example_usage: Quadrature amplitude modulation combines amplitude and phase variations to transmit higher data rates.
linguistic_notes: Zero-Fabrication Policy: Requires fingerspelling M-O-D-U-L-A-T-I-O-N and visual demonstration of message signal riding carrier wave.

definition: An idealized or physical device implementing a Boolean function, performing a logical operation on one or more binary inputs and producing a single binary output.
technical_context: Fabricated using CMOS transistors; NAND and NOR gates serve as universal logic building blocks.
example_usage: An XOR logic gate outputs high only when inputs differ.
linguistic_notes: Two input lines converging into decision gate that opens or closes output line.
handshape: Index fingers converging into dominant flat gate
movement: Inward convergence followed by conditional pass-through

definition: An electronic device that can increase the magnitude of a voltage, current, or power of an input signal.
technical_context: Quantified by gain (A = Vout / Vin), bandwidth, slew rate, and input/output impedances.
example_usage: An operational amplifier configured in negative feedback provides stable closed-loop voltage gain.
linguistic_notes: Candidate sign: Small wave entering triangle envelope and emerging as high-amplitude wave.
handshape: Small sinusoidal wave expanding vertically into large peak
movement: Vertical expansion of hand height moving forward

definition: A material whose electrical conductivity lies between that of a conductor and an insulator.
technical_context: Conductivity modulated by thermal excitation or doping with p-type (acceptor) or n-type (donor) impurities.
example_usage: Silicon is the primary semiconductor material used in integrated circuit manufacturing.
linguistic_notes: Candidate sign: Half-conduct sign balancing conduct/resist states.
handshape: Flat hands oscillating between open (conduct) and closed (insulate)

definition: A specialized transducer that converts radio frequency electric currents into electromagnetic waves in free space, and vice versa.
technical_context: Evaluated by radiation pattern, directivity, gain, polarization, and impedance matching.
example_usage: A dipole antenna radiates electromagnetic energy perpendicular to its conductor axis.
linguistic_notes: Established sign: Vertical mast radiating electromagnetic arcs into space.
handshape: Dominant vertical index finger (mast), non-dominant curved arcs pulsing outward

definition: The difference between the upper and lower frequencies in a continuous band of frequencies, measured in Hertz.
technical_context: Directly constrains maximum channel capacity according to the Shannon-Hartley theorem (C = B * log2(1 + SNR)).
example_usage: Fiber-optic channels provide gigahertz of usable bandwidth with minimal attenuation.
linguistic_notes: Candidate sign: Horizontal measurement between lower and upper frequency boundaries.
handshape: Flat-B hands defining left (f1) and right (f2) limits
movement: Spreading horizontally to indicate wide vs narrow spectrum
non_manual_markers: Pursed lips if narrow, open eyes if wide

definition: An electronic circuit that produces a continuous, repeated, alternating waveform without any external input signal.
technical_context: Requires Barkhausen criteria: loop gain equal to unity and loop phase shift equal to zero or 360 degrees.
example_usage: Quartz crystal oscillators generate stable clock pulses for microcontrollers.
linguistic_notes: Zero-Fabrication Policy: Requires fingerspelling O-S-C-I-L-L-A-T-O-R and waveform generation diagram.

definition: An electrical device that converts alternating current (AC), which periodically reverses direction, to direct current (DC), which flows in only one direction.
technical_context: Configured as half-wave, full-wave center-tapped, or full-wave diode bridge rectifiers followed by capacitive smoothing filters.
example_usage: The full-wave rectifier converts bidirectional AC line power into pulsating DC.
linguistic_notes: Candidate sign: Bidirectional AC wave entering diode block and emerging as flat unidirectional DC line.
handshape: Oscillating wave hand transforming into straight level glide

definition: A device that detects and responds to some type of input from the physical environment (heat, light, motion, pressure).
technical_context: Converts physical quantities into measurable electrical signals (voltage, resistance change, capacitance variation).
example_usage: Piezoelectric sensors convert mechanical pressure variations into electrical voltage spikes.
linguistic_notes: Established sign: Probe surface detecting incoming environmental physical rays.
handshape: Curved claw hand feeling environmental field
movement: Sensitive inward pulse toward sensor plate

definition: An interaction that, when unopposed, changes the motion of an object (mass times acceleration: F = ma).
technical_context: Vector quantity characterized by magnitude, direction, and point of application.
example_usage: A tensile force tends to elongate the steel specimen along its longitudinal axis.
linguistic_notes: Standard ISL sign: Firm pushed fist exerting physical vector pressure.
handshape: Closed S-fist
movement: Powerful forward thrust along directional vector

definition: The phenomenon in which an object changes its position over time with respect to a reference frame.
technical_context: Described mathematically in terms of displacement, distance, velocity, acceleration, speed, and frame of reference.
example_usage: Newton's first law of motion governs the inertia of resting and moving bodies.
linguistic_notes: Continuous smooth sweeping displacement of hands across signing plane.
handshape: Open flat-B hands

definition: The rotational equivalent of linear force, representing the tendency of a force to rotate an object about an axis.
technical_context: Calculated as cross product of position vector and force vector (tau = r x F), measured in Newton-meters (N-m).
example_usage: The engine delivers maximum torque at 3,500 revolutions per minute.
linguistic_notes: Candidate sign: Two-handed twisting moment around central shaft axis.
handshape: Curved C-hands grasping virtual shaft
orientation: Palms opposing each other on rotational perimeter

definition: The force resisting the relative motion of solid surfaces, fluid layers, and material elements sliding against each other.
technical_context: Characterized by coefficient of static friction (mu_s) and kinetic friction (mu_k); F_f = mu * N.
example_usage: Lubricating bearings reduces kinetic friction and minimizes mechanical wear.
linguistic_notes: Established sign: Palms rubbing against each other with resistive friction force.
handshape: Flat open palms contacting firmly

definition: The quantitative property that is transferred to a body or to a physical system, recognizable in the performance of work and in the form of heat and light.
technical_context: Governed by the Law of Conservation of Energy (First Law of Thermodynamics); measured in Joules (J).
example_usage: Potential energy converts into kinetic energy as the pendulum descends.
linguistic_notes: Standard ISL sign: Dynamic power pulse radiating from body center.
handshape: Closed fists bursting open to explosive 5-hands

definition: The amount of energy transferred or converted per unit time (work done divided by time taken: P = W/t).
technical_context: Measured in Watts (W) or Horsepower (hp); 1 hp = 746 Watts.
example_usage: The turbine generates 500 megawatts of electrical power at full flow.
linguistic_notes: Established sign: Biceps contraction indicating mechanical work capability.
handshape: Curved C-hand contacting non-dominant flexed bicep

definition: A physical system using power to apply forces and control movement to perform an intended action.
technical_context: Consists of kinematic linkages, gears, cams, and shafts transmitting mechanical motion and torque.
example_usage: A four-bar linkage is a fundamental mechanism found in many mechanical machines.
linguistic_notes: Standard ISL sign: Interlocking curved fingers rotating like meshing spur gears.
handshape: Bent claw-5 hands with interlocked fingers
orientation: Palms facing body with intermeshed fingers

definition: A rotating circular machine part having cut teeth which mesh with another toothed part to transmit torque and change speed or direction.
technical_context: Governed by gear ratio (N1/N2 = w2/w1 = T2/T1); types include spur, helical, bevel, and worm gears.
example_usage: The planetary gear train provides high reduction ratios in a compact housing.
linguistic_notes: Interlocking finger cogs rotating synchronously in opposite rotational directions.
handshape: Bent fingers meshed as gear teeth

definition: A machine designed to convert one or more forms of energy into mechanical energy.
technical_context: Includes four-stroke IC engines (intake, compression, power, exhaust) operating on Otto or Diesel thermodynamic cycles.
example_usage: The diesel engine relies on high compression ratios to achieve autoignition.
linguistic_notes: Reciprocating vertical piston stroke within cylinder block.
handshape: Dominant fist (piston) reciprocating inside non-dominant cylinder C-hand

definition: The force applied perpendicular to the surface of an object per unit area over which that force is distributed (P = F/A).
technical_context: Measured in Pascals (Pa = N/m^2) or bar; isotropic in static fluids according to Pascal's Principle.
example_usage: Hydrostatic pressure increases linearly with depth in an incompressible liquid.
linguistic_notes: Flat palm pressing down firmly onto flat spatial surface.
handshape: Dominant flat palm pressing downward onto non-dominant flat palm

definition: The directional speed of an object in motion as an indication of its rate of change in position (v = ds/dt).
technical_context: Vector quantity differing from scalar speed; derivative of displacement vector with respect to time.
example_usage: Angular velocity measures the rate of rotation around a fixed axis in radians per second.
linguistic_notes: Rapid linear vector dash across horizontal signing plane.
handshape: V-handshape or flat-B darting forward swiftly

definition: The rate of change of velocity of an object with respect to time (a = dv/dt).
technical_context: Measured in m/s^2; caused by unbalanced net external forces in accordance with Newton's Second Law.
example_usage: Gravitational acceleration at Earth's surface equals approximately 9.81 m/s^2.
linguistic_notes: Candidate sign: Motion beginning slowly and rapidly speeding up across vector line.
handshape: Flat-B hand transitioning from slow drift to rapid surge

definition: The branch of physics that deals with heat, work, and temperature, and their relation to energy, entropy, and physical properties of matter.
technical_context: Governed by the Zeroth, First, Second (entropy non-decrease), and Third laws of thermodynamics.
example_usage: The second law of thermodynamics establishes that heat cannot spontaneously flow from a colder to a hotter body.
linguistic_notes: Compound sign: HEAT (shivering energy) + DYNAMICS (transforming motion). Requires expansion.
handshape: Curved claw hands undulating heat rising into mechanical work piston
movement: Rising thermal wave turning into linear push

definition: The internal force per unit area exerted by neighboring particles of a continuous material upon each other across an internal surface.
technical_context: Contextual Disambiguation: Distinguishes mechanical stress (sigma = F/A) from emotional/psychological stress.
example_usage: Tensile stress causes molecular lattice stretching in ductile metals.
linguistic_notes: Compressive internal force vector acting against crystalline lattice planes.
handshape: Fists squeezing inward against center boundary block

definition: The measure of the deformation of a material body under applied stress, defined as change in length divided by original length (epsilon = delta_L / L).
technical_context: Dimensionless ratio related to stress through Young's Modulus (E = sigma / epsilon) within elastic limits.
example_usage: Elastic strain disappears completely once the applied mechanical load is removed.
linguistic_notes: Candidate sign: Elastic stretching deformation from original baseline length.
handshape: Bent-index fingers hooked together and stretching outward

definition: A rotary mechanical device that extracts energy from a fluid flow and converts it into useful work.
technical_context: Contains rotating blades (impeller/runner) driven by impulse or reaction fluid forces (Euler's turbine equation).
example_usage: Superheated steam expands through high-pressure turbine stages to spin the electrical generator.
linguistic_notes: Candidate sign: Radial blades spinning around a horizontal shaft axis under fluid impulse.
handshape: Curved open-5 hands spinning rapidly around index finger shaft
non_manual_markers: Blowing mouth morpheme representing fluid flow

definition: A measure of a fluid's resistance to gradual deformation by shear stress or tensile stress (fluid thickness).
technical_context: Measured in Pascal-seconds (Pa-s) or poise; Newton's Law of Viscosity: tau = mu * (du/dy).
example_usage: Motor oil with high viscosity maintains a thick protective hydrodynamic film at elevated temperatures.
linguistic_notes: Candidate sign: Sluggish, sticky dripping flow demonstrating internal fluid resistance.
handshape: Curved claw hands pulling apart slowly with sticky resistance

definition: The quantity of motion that an object has, defined as the product of its mass and velocity (p = mv).
technical_context: Conserved in isolated physical systems; impulse equals the integral of net force over time (J = delta_p).
example_usage: In an elastic collision, both total momentum and kinetic energy are conserved.
linguistic_notes: Zero-Fabrication Policy: Requires fingerspelling M-O-M-E-N-T-U-M followed by mass-velocity product classifier.

definition: The movement of thermal energy from one thing to another of different temperature (conduction, convection, radiation).
technical_context: Governed by Fourier's law of conduction (q = -k*grad_T), Newton's law of cooling, and Stefan-Boltzmann radiation law.
example_usage: Heat exchangers maximize conductive and convective heat transfer between two fluid streams.
linguistic_notes: Candidate sign: Thermal energy flowing from high-temp locus A to low-temp locus B.
handshape: Curved thermal hands migrating across temperature gradient

definition: The branch of physics concerned with the mechanics of fluids (liquids, gases, and plasmas) and the forces on them.
technical_context: Modeled mathematically by the Navier-Stokes equations governing mass, momentum, and energy conservation.
example_usage: Computational fluid mechanics models laminar and turbulent air flow around turbine airfoils.
linguistic_notes: Compound sign: FLUID (flowing liquid ripples) + MECHANICS (gear meshing).
handshape: Wavy fluid ripple transitioning into gear interlocking
movement: Horizontal wave into circular gear lock

definition: An arrangement and organization of interrelated elements in an engineered object, such as a building, bridge, or dam.
technical_context: Designed to safely transmit static dead loads and dynamic live loads into foundations without structural collapse.
example_usage: Truss bridges distribute structural forces through triangular axial members.
linguistic_notes: Two-handed framework construction building upward vertical grid planes.
handshape: Bent-B hands forming vertical and horizontal framing planes

definition: The element of a structure that connects it to the ground, transferring loads from the superstructure to the earth.
technical_context: Includes shallow foundations (spread footings, raft slabs) and deep foundations (drilled shafts, driven piles).
example_usage: Pile foundations transfer high building loads down to dense bedrock strata.
linguistic_notes: Standard ISL sign: Firm horizontal ground bedrock base supporting superstructure load.
handshape: Flat non-dominant forearm (bedrock) with dominant fist planting solid contact downward

definition: A composite material composed of fine and coarse aggregate bonded together with a fluid cement that hardens over time.
technical_context: Exceptional compressive strength (20-50 MPa); reinforced with embedded steel rebar to resist tensile forces.
example_usage: Prestressed concrete minimizes tensile cracking under severe bending loads.

handshape: Claw hands mixing aggregates into solid flat surface
movement: Kneading motion followed by flat firm smoothing

definition: A structural element that primarily resists loads applied laterally to the beam's axis through bending moments.

example_usage: A simply supported beam develops maximum bending moments at its midspan under uniform loads.
linguistic_notes: Flat horizontal structural member bridging two vertical spatial column supports.
handshape: Flat-B hands positioned horizontally spanning two vertical index posts

definition: A vertical structural member designed to transmit a compressive load from the superstructure to the foundation.

example_usage: Reinforced concrete columns carry vertical axial loads from upper building floors.
linguistic_notes: Vertical cylindrical pillar rising from foundation base to roof beam.
handshape: Curved-C hands outlining vertical cylinder perimeter

definition: Forces, deformations, or accelerations applied to structure components or their elements.

linguistic_notes: Heavy downward weight pressing upon horizontal load-bearing beam.

definition: An unaligned force acting on one part of a body in a direction and upon another part in an opposite direction, causing parallel sliding planes.
technical_context: Produces diagonal tension cracks in concrete beams; mitigated by vertical steel stirrups.
example_usage: Stirrups resist high shear forces near the beam support columns.
linguistic_notes: Candidate sign: Flat palms sliding across each other in opposite parallel directions.
handshape: Flat-B hands touching edge to edge

definition: The branch of engineering mechanics that describes the behavior of soils under applied loads, water seepage, and compaction.
technical_context: Analyzes Terzaghi's effective stress principle (sigma' = sigma - u), permeability, and shear strength (Mohr-Coulomb criterion).
example_usage: Soil mechanics tests determine the bearing capacity of clay soil prior to foundation excavation.
linguistic_notes: Compound sign: SOIL (crumbling earth grains) + MECHANICS (structural behavior).
handshape: Fingers rubbing earth texture then forming stability frame
movement: Textural crumble then structural base placement

definition: The technique, profession, and science of determining the terrestrial two-dimensional or three-dimensional positions of points and the distances and angles between them.
technical_context: Employs optical theodolites, total stations, GPS/GNSS receivers, and LiDAR for topographic mapping and boundary demarcation.
example_usage: Surveying teams establish precise horizontal benchmarks before highway grading begins.
linguistic_notes: Established sign: Peering through theodolite telescope across distant land stakes.
handshape: Curved C-hand forming optical eye telescope
movement: Sightline alignment toward distant target stake

definition: Steel bars, mesh, or wires embedded in concrete to provide tensile strength that plain concrete lacks.
technical_context: High-yield deformed bars (Fe 415 / Fe 500) ribbed to ensure strong mechanical bond with surrounding cured concrete matrix.
example_usage: Deformed steel reinforcement bars prevent catastrophic brittle tension failure in bridge decks.
linguistic_notes: Candidate sign: Inserting ribbed steel grid skeleton inside concrete formwork.
handshape: Interlocking grid fingers locking inside concrete casing
movement: Firm insertion and locking mesh motion

definition: A binder, a substance used for construction that sets, hardens, and adheres to other materials to bind them together.
technical_context: Hydraulic binder produced by calcining limestone and clay; undergoes exothermic hydration reactions producing calcium silicate hydrates.
example_usage: Ordinary Portland cement hydrates to form a dense impervious crystalline matrix.
linguistic_notes: Powder pouring and mixing with water into adhesive binding paste.
handshape: Sprinkling fingertips followed by flat adhesive smoothing

definition: A workable paste which hardens to bind building blocks such as stones, bricks, and concrete masonry units together.
technical_context: Mixture of sand, a binder (such as cement or lime), and water; fills gaps and bonds structural masonry units.
example_usage: Masons apply a 10 mm bed of cement mortar between successive brick courses.
linguistic_notes: Candidate sign: Trowel spreading adhesive bed between brick layers.
handshape: Flat trowel hand sweeping paste between stacked brick blocks

definition: A structure designed and constructed to resist the lateral pressure of soil when there is a desired change in ground elevation.
technical_context: Resists active lateral earth pressure (Rankine or Coulomb theory); checked against overturning, sliding, and bearing capacity failure.
example_usage: The cantilever retaining wall holds back unstable hillside soils adjacent to the roadway.
linguistic_notes: Candidate sign: Vertical wall holding back lateral sloping soil pressure.
handshape: Vertical dominant palm resisting lateral soil push from non-dominant hand
orientation: Dominant palm facing sideways to block

definition: The scientific study of the movement, distribution, and management of water on Earth, including the hydrologic cycle and water resources.
technical_context: Analyzes precipitation runoff, hydrographs, groundwater infiltration, flood recurrence intervals, and river basin hydraulics.
example_usage: Hydrology models estimate peak 100-year flood discharge to dimension bridge spillways.
linguistic_notes: Compound sign: WATER (W-handshape at chin) + RAIN/RIVER (circulating water flow cycle).
handshape: W-hand at chin then undulating river flow lines
movement: Chin tap into flowing stream progression

definition: The natural or artificial removal of a surface's water and sub-surface water from an area with excess water.
technical_context: Includes storm sewers, swales, retention ponds, and culverts designed using Manning's open channel flow formula.
example_usage: Inadequate roadside drainage leads to subgrade saturation and asphalt pavement rutting.
linguistic_notes: Water gathering and channeling downward through culvert outlet.
handshape: Open-5 hands funneling downward into narrow stream channel

definition: The process in which a stress applied to a soil causes densification as air is displaced from the pores between soil grains.
technical_context: Optimized by identifying optimum moisture content (OMC) via Standard or Modified Proctor compaction tests.
example_usage: Vibratory rollers achieve 95% standard Proctor compaction on the highway embankment.
linguistic_notes: Candidate sign: Heavy downward tamping compressing porous soil into dense solid stratum.
handshape: Heavy flat fists tamping down repeatedly

definition: The maximum stress that a material can withstand while being stretched or pulled before breaking.
technical_context: Evaluated via universal testing machines (UTM) to generate stress-strain curves exhibiting yield and ultimate strength.
example_usage: Structural steel provides high tensile strength of over 400 MPa.
linguistic_notes: Candidate sign: Opposing horizontal pull testing breaking resistance threshold.
handshape: Hooked fingers pulling outward with high tension

definition: A system of structural members arranged to provide stability and resist lateral wind and earthquake forces on building frames.
technical_context: Includes diagonal X-bracing, chevron bracing, and K-bracing converting lateral drift forces into axial tension/compression.
example_usage: Steel cross-bracing prevents lateral sway during high windstorms.
linguistic_notes: Zero-Fabrication Policy: Requires fingerspelling B-R-A-C-I-N-G and cross-diagonal structural classifier depiction.

definition: The downward movement of the ground or foundation of a structure as the underlying soil compresses under building weight.
technical_context: Differentiated into immediate elastic settlement, primary consolidation settlement (pore water expulsion), and secondary creep.
example_usage: Differential settlement across building corners can produce severe structural wall cracks.
linguistic_notes: Candidate sign: Foundation base sinking slowly into underlying soil stratum.
handshape: Flat horizontal foundation settling unevenly downward

definition: The substructure at the ends of a bridge span or dam whereon the structure's superstructure rests or abuts.
technical_context: Acts simultaneously as vertical superstructure support and lateral earth retaining wall for bridge approach fills.
example_usage: The reinforced concrete abutment anchors the bridge girder into the riverbank hillside.
linguistic_notes: Zero-Fabrication Policy: Requires fingerspelling A-B-U-T-M-E-N-T and bridge endpoint support diagram.

definition: The set of physical phenomena associated with the presence and motion of matter that has a property of electric charge.
technical_context: Governed by Maxwell's equations; generated at central stations and transmitted via high-voltage three-phase grids.
example_usage: Hydroelectric power plants generate clean electricity using water turbines.
linguistic_notes: Standard ISL sign: Curved bent index fingers tapping together like electric sparking contacts.
handshape: Bent-X fingers meeting rapidly

definition: A passive component that transfers electrical energy from one electrical circuit to another through the process of electromagnetic induction.
technical_context: Governed by turns ratio (V1/V2 = N1/N2 = I2/I1); changes AC voltage levels without changing frequency.
example_usage: Step-up transformers increase transmission voltage to 400 kV to minimize I^2*R heat losses.
linguistic_notes: Candidate sign: Primary coil inducing voltage into secondary coil across iron core.
handshape: Curved-C hands facing each other representing primary and secondary windings
movement: Magnetic inductive transfer pulse across gap

definition: An electrical machine that converts electrical energy into mechanical rotational energy.
technical_context: Operates via interaction between magnetic field and winding currents (Lorentz force law) producing shaft torque.
example_usage: Three-phase induction motors are the workhorses of industrial manufacturing.
linguistic_notes: Standard ISL sign: Hand rotating rapidly like an electric motor rotor shaft.
handshape: Fist rotating around central axis inside open stator palm

definition: A device that converts motive power (mechanical energy) into electrical power for use in an external circuit.
technical_context: Driven by steam, hydro, or wind turbines to induce AC voltage in stator windings via rotating magnetic rotor poles.
example_usage: Synchronous generators at the dam produce three-phase power synchronized at 50 Hz.
linguistic_notes: Manual mechanical rotation input generating outward electric power output.
handshape: Hand cranking rotation followed by electric sparks radiating out

definition: A network of electrical components deployed to supply, transfer, and use electric power.
technical_context: Consists of generation, transmission network, substations, distribution networks, and industrial/residential loads.
example_usage: Power system state estimation monitors voltage stability across the national grid.
linguistic_notes: Compound sign: ELECTRICITY + NETWORK-GRID spanning regional nodes.
handshape: Electricity sparks transitioning to widespread linked power towers
movement: Spark tap into expansive grid network layout

definition: An electric current which periodically reverses direction and changes its magnitude continuously with time in contrast to direct current.
technical_context: Sinusoidal waveform (i(t) = I_peak * sin(omega*t + phi)); standard transmission frequency in India is 50 Hz.
example_usage: Alternating current allows easy voltage step-up and step-down using electromagnetic transformers.
linguistic_notes: Alternating bidirectional wave motion oscillating forward and backward in time.
handshape: V-hands or flat hands undulating in periodic alternating cycle

definition: One-directional flow of electric charge, produced by sources such as batteries, thermocouples, solar cells, and commutated dynamos.
technical_context: Constant voltage over time (frequency = 0 Hz); utilized in battery energy storage, electronics, and HVDC transmission.
example_usage: Photovoltaic solar panels produce direct current that is converted by an inverter into AC.
linguistic_notes: Straight unwavering unidirectional linear charge flow along conductor path.
handshape: Index finger tracing dead-straight horizontal line

definition: The final stage in the delivery of electricity to end consumers, stepping down transmission voltage to medium and low levels (11 kV, 415 V, 230 V).
technical_context: Carried out via radial, ring main, or interconnected distribution feeders with pole-mounted transformers.
example_usage: Distribution transformers step down 11 kV feeder voltage to 415 V three-phase for residential consumers.
linguistic_notes: Central power hub dividing outward into multiple localized branches.
handshape: Fingers spreading outward from single point into multiple branch directions

definition: The bulk movement of electrical energy from a generating site, such as a power plant, to an electrical substation.
technical_context: Conducted at extra-high voltages (132 kV to 765 kV AC, or +/- 800 kV HVDC) on steel lattice towers to minimize current and resistive losses.
example_usage: Long-distance high-voltage AC transmission lines connect remote solar parks to urban load centers.
linguistic_notes: High tower structures with long-distance horizontal wire lines spanning across space.
handshape: High towers represented by vertical hand, other hand shooting long wire beams forward

definition: An automatically operated electrical switch designed to protect an electrical circuit from damage caused by excess current from an overload or short circuit.
technical_context: Interrupts high fault currents (tens of kiloamperes); utilizes arc-extinguishing media such as SF6 gas, vacuum, or oil.
example_usage: The SF6 circuit breaker tripped within 40 milliseconds to isolate the busbar fault.
linguistic_notes: Snapping open of electrical contact to extinguish fault current arc.
handshape: Contacting knuckles snapping apart forcefully to break connection
non_manual_markers: Sharp head snap matching trip instant

definition: An electrically operated switch that senses electrical faults and commands circuit breakers to trip when parameters exceed thresholds.
technical_context: Includes overcurrent, differential, and distance impedance relays implemented on modern microprocessor numerical platforms.
example_usage: The differential relay detected internal transformer winding faults and sent a trip signal.
linguistic_notes: Candidate sign: Electromagnetic sensing coil commanding secondary circuit trigger switch.
handshape: Sensing coil triggering switch contact
movement: Sense followed by rapid contact switch

definition: The production of an electromotive force across an electrical conductor in a changing magnetic field.
technical_context: Discovered by Michael Faraday; EMF = -N * (dPhi/dt) with negative sign denoting Lenz's Law of opposing magnetic flux.
example_usage: Electromagnetic induction in the stator windings generates terminal AC voltage.
linguistic_notes: Candidate sign: Moving magnetic field causing contactless electron current generation in adjacent conductor.
handshape: Oscillating magnetic field hovering over conductor loop causing circular current
movement: Field hover causing circular internal flow
orientation: Palms facing each other across air gap

definition: A measurement of the total magnetic field which passes through a given surface area, measured in Webers (Wb).
technical_context: Calculated as surface integral of magnetic B-field (Phi = integral B dot dA); concentrated by high-permeability iron cores.
example_usage: Magnetic flux density reaches saturation at 1.8 Tesla in silicon steel transformer cores.
linguistic_notes: Candidate sign: Parallel magnetic field lines piercing perpendicular spatial surface area.
handshape: Open fingers representing flux lines penetrating non-dominant flat loop

definition: Part of an electrical generation, transmission, and distribution system where voltage is transformed from high to low, or the reverse.
technical_context: Features high-voltage busbars, power transformers, gas-insulated switchgear (GIS), circuit breakers, and protection panels.
example_usage: The 400/220 kV substation interlinks regional transmission lines with city ring feeders.
linguistic_notes: Complex industrial compound: Large transformers + busbars + incoming/outgoing high-voltage lines.
handshape: Square yard perimeter holding central transformer and power towers
movement: Perimeter outline and incoming wire links

definition: A power electronic device or circuitry that changes direct current (DC) to alternating current (AC).
technical_context: Utilizes high-frequency PWM switching of IGBTs or SiC MOSFETs to reconstruct low-distortion AC sine waves.
example_usage: The solar grid-tied inverter converts DC from rooftop panels into 230 V AC synchronized with the grid.
linguistic_notes: Candidate sign: Straight DC input flipped into periodic sinusoidal AC output.
handshape: Straight line hand turning 180 degrees into sine wave oscillation
orientation: Palms flipping from down to waving

definition: An interconnected network for delivering electricity from producers to consumers across an entire country or region.
technical_context: Synchronized nationwide AC network operating at unified frequency (50 Hz) managed by Load Despatch Centres.
example_usage: India's National Grid operates as 'One Nation, One Grid, One Frequency'.
linguistic_notes: Expansive interconnected mesh of electrical nodes spanning broad geographic signing space.
handshape: Interlocking grid fingers linking across broad horizontal space

definition: The measure of the total opposition that a circuit presents to a current when a voltage is applied in alternating current circuits.
technical_context: Complex quantity: Z = R + jX (Resistance plus imaginary Reactance), measured in Ohms with phase angle theta.
example_usage: Impedance matching between source and load maximizes real power transfer.
linguistic_notes: Zero-Fabrication Policy: Requires fingerspelling I-M-P-E-D-A-N-C-E and complex R + jX phasor explanation.

definition: A representation of a sinusoidal function whose amplitude, frequency, and phase are time-invariant, represented as a rotating complex vector.
technical_context: Transforms differential equations in time domain into algebraic linear equations in frequency domain.
example_usage: Phasor measurement units (PMUs) synchronize voltage phase angles across wide-area power networks.
linguistic_notes: Zero-Fabrication Policy: Requires fingerspelling P-H-A-S-O-R and rotating vector diagram.

definition: A direct electrical connection between an electrical circuit or equipment chassis and the physical earth.
technical_context: Provides a low-impedance path for fault currents to safely trigger breakers, protecting humans against shock hazards.
example_usage: Equipment chassis earthing prevents touch-potential shock hazards during insulation breakdown.
linguistic_notes: Wire conductor connecting downward directly into physical earth soil ground.
handshape: Index finger driving downward into flat non-dominant earth palm
movement: Direct vertical downward contact stroke into ground

definition: The component of an electrical machine that carries alternating current and develops electromotive force or torque.
technical_context: Rotating rotor in DC machines; stationary stator in large synchronous AC alternators.
example_usage: Armature reaction distorts the main field flux and shifts the neutral magnetic plane.
linguistic_notes: Candidate sign: Cylindrical slotted rotor core wound with copper coils rotating in magnetic field.
handshape: Cylindrical rotor frame with wire wraps rotating in air gap
movement: Coil winding motion around central cylinder
